articleHeadline: Dengue in Thailand: Symptoms and Warning Signs That Need Urgent Care
articleSummary: On 2026-10-02, dengue remains a year-round risk in Thailand, transmitted by Aedes mosquitoes that bite during the day; peaks during the rainy season. Dengue typically begins with sudden high fever, headache, eye pain, muscle and joint aches, nausea, vomiting, rash, or swollen glands, with illness lasting 2–7 days in the febrile phase. As fever falls, a short critical phase can occur within 24–48 hours, during which condition may worsen. Seek urgent medical care for warning signs: severe abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, bleeding (nose/gums, vomit, black stools, heavy menses, blood in urine), rapid breathing, dizziness, confusion, drowsiness, or very little urine. Do not assume recovery with a lower fever. For fever or pain, use acetaminophen (paracetamol) as directed; avoid aspirin/ibuprofen due to bleeding risk. Dengue testing varies by illness day: molecular or NS1 early; antibody tests later; a negative early result does not rule out dengue; follow clinician guidance.

articleHeadline: Rainy-Season Surveillance in Yangon Reveals Shifting Respiratory Virus
articleSummary: Yangon, Myanmar, rainy-season molecular surveillance of acute respiratory infections in outpatients at two Yangon hospitals (June–November 2024; n=646) found pathogens in 548 cases (84.8%). Of 331 rapid diagnostic tests (RDT)-positive samples, RT-PCR confirmed influenza A(H3N2) (40.5%), RSV A (21.5%), influenza B/Victoria (20.2%), and influenza A(H1N1)pdm09 (0.3%). Among 315 RDT-negative samples, the BioFire FilmArray panel detected rhinovirus/enterovirus in 42.5% and human metapneumovirus (hMPV) in 15.2%. Co-infections were identified in 35 of 229 BioFire-positive samples (15.3%). Median age was 3.7 years. Temporal patterns showed influenza peaking in July–August and RSV peaking in September, indicating distinct tropical-seasonality trajectories. The study underscores substantial viral etiology and pathogen diversity driving pediatric respiratory illness and highlights the value of multiplex molecular testing alongside rapid assays for sustained surveillance in settings with limited diagnostics.
